prompt: What does /64 describe in an IPv6 address?
options: The first 64 bits identify the prefix.
The final 64 bits identify the prefix.
The subnet contains exactly 64 addresses.
The address contains a total of 64 bits.
explanation: A prefix length counts the retained leading bits; 128 minus that length gives the remaining bits.

whyWrong.1: The prefix consists of the leading bits.
whyWrong.2: A prefix length is a bit count, not an address count.
whyWrong.3: The complete address still contains 128 bits.

prompt: What is true of fd12:3456:789a:1::a1/64?
options: It is multicast because it begins with f.
It is a unique local address for routed private connectivity.
It is link-local and can never cross a router.
It is global unicast intended for normal public Internet allocation.
explanation: fd falls inside the locally generated half of ULA fc00::/7. ULA can be routed within suitable private networks but is not intended for global Internet routing.

whyWrong.0: Multicast begins ff, not fd.
whyWrong.2: Link-local belongs to fe80::/10.
whyWrong.3: The fd prefix identifies locally generated ULA, not globally allocated Internet space.

prompt: Which TWO groups identify all IPv6 nodes and all IPv6 routers, respectively, on the local link?
explanation: ff02::1 is all-nodes and ff02::2 is all-routers, both with link-local multicast scope.

whyWrong.2: ff05::2 has site scope, not the requested link scope.
whyWrong.3: This is a solicited-node group, not the all-nodes group.

prompt: The same unicast-format service address is assigned to instances in several locations and routing sends each packet to one preferred instance. What is this?
options: Broadcast to all locations
Multicast, requiring the address to start ff
Anycast; selection follows the routing system's preferred path
A duplicate that is forbidden even across separate routed links
explanation: Anycast uses one shared address at multiple locations with routing choosing an instance. Its text has no unique anycast prefix.

whyWrong.0: IPv6 has no broadcast addressing type.
whyWrong.1: Multicast is group delivery and uses multicast-format addresses; this scenario is anycast.
whyWrong.3: Deliberate anycast across locations is a defined use, not an ordinary same-link unicast conflict.

prompt: The same MAC is available, but an automatically addressed host does not contain ff:fe in its identifier. Which conclusion is justified?
options: IPv6 cannot operate without a modified EUI-64 identifier.
Another valid identifier method may be in use.
The host must have obtained its address from stateful DHCPv6.
The absence of ff:fe proves Duplicate Address Detection failed.
explanation: SLAAC can use stable opaque or other supported identifiers; not all IIDs embed the MAC. Address appearance alone does not establish a fault.

whyWrong.0: Modified EUI-64 is one method, not a universal requirement.
whyWrong.2: SLAAC can use identifiers that do not embed the MAC, so the suffix does not establish DHCPv6 use.
whyWrong.3: DAD tests local uniqueness; it does not require a particular identifier pattern.

prompt: A host obtains an address and DNS information from stateful DHCPv6. It has no manual routes. What ordinarily supplies its default router?
options: A Router Advertisement with a usable nonzero router lifetime
The DHCPv6 address lease always includes the default-router option.
The host uses its DHCPv6-provided DNS server as the router.
The prefix L flag identifies the router by itself.
explanation: The host learns a default router from RA, independently of how DHCPv6 supplied its address and DNS.

whyWrong.1: Ordinary DHCPv6 address assignment does not supply the IPv6 default router; that normally comes from RA.
whyWrong.2: DNS configuration identifies a name server, not the default router.
whyWrong.3: L provides on-link prefix information; the RA source and router lifetime determine default-router information.

prompt: Which TWO Neighbor Discovery statements are correct?
options: Address-resolution NS messages can target a solicited-node multicast group.
Every NS is broadcast to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.
A unicast NS can be used to verify a known neighbor's reachability.
Every stale neighbor entry proves a failed device.
explanation: ND distinguishes initial address resolution from reachability confirmation. NS can be multicast or unicast depending on the operation.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 has no IP broadcast; ordinary IPv6 multicast uses multicast delivery.
whyWrong.3: Stale means reachability is not recently confirmed, not that failure is proven.

prompt: A fresh IOS interface has no configured IPv6 address. Which single interface command enables IPv6 processing and an automatic link-local address without adding a global prefix?
options: ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 enable
ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64
explanation: ipv6 enable provides the requested interface behavior without supplying a global prefix.

whyWrong.0: That is a global forwarding command, not this interface-addressing instruction.
whyWrong.2: This also configures a global-form address, contrary to the requested result.
whyWrong.3: This configures IPv4.

prompt: Which is the canonical spelling of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:000a?
explanation: Each zero run has two groups. Canonical spelling compresses the leftmost tied run and removes leading zeros within the remaining groups.

whyWrong.0: Two double-colon sequences make expansion ambiguous.
whyWrong.1: This is valid but compresses the rightmost of two equal zero runs.
whyWrong.2: Moving a zero into the 1 group changes the bits.

prompt: Which is the canonical representation of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0a00:0000:0001?
explanation: Remove leading zeros and compress the longest run of three zero groups. The trailing zeros in a00 remain significant.

whyWrong.1: Changing a00 to a changes its numeric value.
whyWrong.2: Two double-colon sequences are invalid.
whyWrong.3: This is valid but does not use the canonical compression of the longest zero run.

prompt: An example allocation is 2001:db8:5c00::/56. How many /64s fit, and which is the last?
explanation: 64−56 leaves 8 subnet bits: 256 choices. They occupy the low byte of the fourth group, from 00 through ff.

whyWrong.0: 16 choices correspond to four extra bits, as with /60 to /64.
whyWrong.1: This changes retained bits in the third group.
whyWrong.3: The /56 fixes the upper byte of the fourth group; all 16 bits are not available.

prompt: A site has 2001:db8:1200:3400::/56. Which proposed /64 is outside that allocation?
explanation: The /56 retains 34 in the high byte of the fourth group. The /64 choices run from 3400 through 34ff; 3500 changes a retained bit.

whyWrong.0: This is the last /64 in the allocation.
whyWrong.1: The fixed first byte of the fourth group is 34.
whyWrong.3: This is the first /64 in the allocation.

prompt: What is the prefix containing 2001:db8:5:c7f2::1/60?
explanation: A /60 retains the first three groups and the first three hex digits of the fourth. Zero the last digit and all following bits.

whyWrong.1: c700 discards retained prefix bits.
whyWrong.2: The low fourth-group digit is outside /60 and must be zero in the network address.
whyWrong.3: This removes the entire retained c7f part.

prompt: What /61 prefix contains 2001:db8:7:ab3d::25/61?
explanation: After the first 60 bits, /61 retains one bit of the final hex digit. Hex d is binary 1101: retain its first bit and clear the last three, obtaining 1000, or 8. The block covers ab38 through ab3f.

whyWrong.0: This leaves nonzero bits outside the prefix.
whyWrong.1: A /61 boundary must clear the final three bits of the fourth group.
whyWrong.2: That clears a bit which /61 retains; it covers ab30 through ab37.

prompt: An isolated site needs 20 distinct /64 LANs. Which smallest allocation from this list can contain them?
options: /61, providing 8 distinct /64 prefixes
/64, providing one distinct /64 prefix
/60, providing 16 distinct /64 prefixes
/59, providing 32 distinct /64 prefixes
explanation: Five additional subnet bits provide 2^5 = 32 choices. A /59 is therefore the longest prefix, and smallest block, among these sufficient choices.

whyWrong.0: Eight is fewer than twenty.
whyWrong.1: One LAN prefix cannot meet twenty distinct /64 allocations.
whyWrong.2: Sixteen is fewer than twenty.

prompt: MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e uses modified EUI-64 on 2001:db8:10:1::/64. Which address results?
explanation: Insert ff:fe after the first three MAC bytes and invert the first byte's U/L bit, changing 00 to 02. Regrouping yields 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e.

whyWrong.0: The first byte's U/L bit was not inverted.
whyWrong.1: The inserted bytes are in the wrong position.
whyWrong.3: EUI-64 does not assign the convenient suffix ::1.

prompt: Derive the modified EUI-64 identifier from MAC 02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee.
options: 04aa:bbff:fecc:ddee
00aa:bbcc:fffe:ddee
02aa:bbff:fecc:ddee
00aa:bbff:fecc:ddee
explanation: 02 XOR 02 is 00. Insert ff:fe between bb and cc, then regroup the eight bytes into four groups.

whyWrong.0: Invert the U/L bit with XOR 02; do not always add 2.
whyWrong.1: Insert ff:fe after the first three MAC bytes, not after the fourth.
whyWrong.2: This inserts ff:fe but fails to invert the U/L bit.

prompt: Which solicited-node multicast group corresponds to 2001:db8:4::ab12:3456?
explanation: The last 24 bits are 12:3456. Combine those bits with the solicited-node multicast prefix.

whyWrong.0: The low 24 bits belong after the fixed ff02::1:ff00:0/104 prefix.
whyWrong.2: This discards the upper byte of the final 24 bits.
whyWrong.3: This takes the wrong 24 bits.

prompt: R1 has FE80::1 on Gi0/0 and on Gi0/1, which connect to separate isolated LANs. Which two statements are correct? Choose two.
options: A diagnostic targeting FE80::1 must identify the intended link.
DAD on Gi0/0 checks for the duplicate on Gi0/1.
R1 must forward packets addressed to FE80::1 between those LANs.
The two identical address texts can be valid because the links differ.
A link-local address must be globally unique across the whole enterprise.
explanation: Scope includes the link. Text alone cannot distinguish repeated link-local addresses on separate interfaces.

whyWrong.1: DAD checks the local link, not other routed links.
whyWrong.2: Routers do not forward link-local-addressed traffic onto another link.
whyWrong.4: Its required uniqueness is within its link.

prompt: Which interface command explicitly creates an EUI-64-derived address in 2001:db8:acad:2::/64?
options: ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::1/64
ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
ipv6 enable
explanation: The eui-64 keyword instructs IOS to build the interface identifier from the interface MAC.

whyWrong.0: This manually sets ::1 rather than deriving an identifier.
whyWrong.2: This sets a link-local address.
whyWrong.3: This enables processing and link-local addressing without the requested global prefix.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
RA source: fe80::1; Router Lifetime: 1800 seconds
Header: M=0, O=1
Prefix: 2001:db8:acad:1::/64; A=1, L=1
No RA DNS option. A working stateless DHCPv6 server supplies DNS.

prompt: A client supports SLAAC and stateless DHCPv6, with no manual DNS settings. What behavior is supported by the shown RA and available server?
options: DHCPv6 must provide the default router.
A=1 forces the host to derive its identifier from its MAC.
The host cannot form an address without M=1.
SLAAC address, DHCPv6 DNS, and RA-learned default router.
explanation: The A-enabled /64 permits SLAAC. O indicates other DHCPv6 information, supplied here by a server. The nonzero RA lifetime permits the advertised router as default.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary default-router discovery uses RA, not DHCPv6.
whyWrong.1: SLAAC does not require the EUI-64 identifier method.
whyWrong.2: M is not required for SLAAC.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete relevant R1 settings:
no ipv6 unicast-routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
 no shutdown
Interface up/up; no other advertising router exists.

prompt: Automatic PCs receive only link-local addresses. The router answers a manually addressed PC on the local LAN. What missing prerequisite is directly shown?
options: IPv6 forwarding/router operation has not been enabled globally.
IPv6 processing has not been enabled on the addressed interface.
The manual global address must first be replaced by an EUI-64 address.
The RA managed-address flag must be set for all SLAAC clients.
explanation: The displayed no ipv6 unicast-routing setting leaves the router acting as an IPv6 endpoint instead of the advertising/forwarding router needed here.

whyWrong.1: The configured IPv6 address and successful local ping show interface IPv6 processing is present.
whyWrong.2: The manual /64 address is valid; its derivation method does not enable global router operation.
whyWrong.3: SLAAC does not require the managed-address flag; that flag describes DHCPv6 address configuration.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 2001:db8:acad:1::10/64
PC-A gateway: 2001:db8:acad:10::1
R1 Gi0/0 up/up:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1
No router owns 2001:db8:acad:10::1.

prompt: PC-A's manually configured gateway does not answer. Which evidenced mismatch should be corrected?
options: The PC must obtain its gateway from DHCPv6 instead of using the documented manual address.
The PC should widen its prefix to /48 while retaining the gateway text.
The PC cannot use a manually configured global-form gateway.
The PC names acad:10::1, but the actual router address is acad:1::1.
explanation: The displayed gateway has fourth group 10 rather than 1 and does not match the configured router address. Verify the intended gateway rather than assuming every failure is caused by routing.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary DHCPv6 does not supply the default router, and a correct on-link manual gateway can be valid.
whyWrong.1: Widening a prefix cannot make the router own the mistyped gateway address.
whyWrong.2: A manually configured on-link global unicast gateway can be valid; the fault is the specific incorrect address.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete Gi0/1 address configuration:
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
Displayed addresses:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:2:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

prompt: Hosts use 2001:db8:acad:2::1 as a manual gateway. What does this excerpt establish?
options: The eui-64 keyword guarantees ::1 also exists.
The manual link-local address also creates a global address with the same ::1 suffix.
Clearing the PC neighbor cache will create the missing ::1 address on R1.
The derived address exists, but the expected ::1 is absent.
explanation: The listed global address is not ::1. Repair the addressing plan or gateway expectation; do not assume EUI-64 creates both addresses.

whyWrong.0: EUI-64 supplies the derived suffix, not an additional ::1.
whyWrong.1: A manual link-local address does not assign a matching global address.
whyWrong.2: Cache refresh cannot assign an address absent from the router configuration.

prompt: What action is justified by a duplicate-address indication on a newly assigned host address?
options: Clear the router neighbor cache and assume the address is unique.
Investigate which device on this link already uses that address before assigning it.
Change the address from uppercase to lowercase.
Disable DAD so both hosts can use the planned address.
explanation: DAD is a local uniqueness check. Preserve the evidence and correct the conflicting assignment, rather than hiding it.

whyWrong.0: Clearing cached bindings does not remove another device using the address.
whyWrong.2: Case changes the spelling, not the address bits.
whyWrong.3: Bypassing the conflict check does not resolve the ordinary same-link unicast conflict.

prompt: What explains the host having an address but no automatically learned default router?
options: The prefix can supply an address; router lifetime zero offers no default router.
The host must use the DNS server as its default router.
A=1 means the host must ignore the router-lifetime field.
A /64 address forces the RA sender to be installed as a default router.
explanation: The address may be formed from the autonomous prefix with its usable lifetime. A router lifetime of zero does not offer the RA sender as a default router.

whyWrong.1: DNS server information does not designate the router.
whyWrong.2: A is a prefix option flag and does not override the RA router lifetime.
whyWrong.3: Address assignment and default-router selection use different RA information.

exhibit.title: RA address and router lifetimes (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Fresh host; no static gateway and no other RA sender.
RA source FE80::1, router lifetime 0
Prefix 2001:db8:24::/64, A=1, L=1, usable prefix lifetimes
Host has 2001:db8:24::25/64; default-router list is empty.

prompt: Which conclusion follows from this addressing evidence?
options: L=0 invalidates the /64 and prevents any address from being formed.
SLAAC can form the address, but this PIO does not assert that the prefix is on-link.
A=1 also implies L=1, so the host must resolve every same-prefix destination directly.
The host must replace its prefix length with /128 because L=0.
explanation: Address assignment and on-link determination are separate. Other valid on-link information could exist, but this particular PIO does not supply it.

whyWrong.0: L describes on-link information; A permits autonomous address formation.
whyWrong.2: The autonomous and on-link flags are independent.
whyWrong.3: The flag does not rewrite the autonomous address prefix length.

exhibit.title: Independent A and L flags (exercise)
exhibit.text:
RA source FE80::1, router lifetime 1800
Prefix information: 2001:db8:25::/64, A=1, L=0
Prefix lifetimes are usable; no other on-link information is supplied.

prompt: Which is the smallest addressing repair consistent with the plan and evidence?
options: Change PC-B gateway to R1 LAN 1 global address.
Change both router LANs to /48 to make the mistaken host prefix fit.
Change PC-B to 2001:db8:26:2::20/64 and keep its link-local gateway.
Replace the gateway with ::1 because it always means the local router.
explanation: The link and router gateway are present on LAN 2. The PC global prefix belongs to the other LAN, so correct that field without widening both subnets.

whyWrong.0: That address is not an on-link gateway for PC-B LAN 2.
whyWrong.1: This overlaps the separate routed LANs and abandons the /64 plan.
whyWrong.3: ::1 is the host itself, not its default router.

exhibit.title: Approved and configured LAN prefixes (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Plan: LAN 1 = 2001:db8:26:1::/64; LAN 2 = 2001:db8:26:2::/64
R1 LAN 2: 2001:db8:26:2::1/64, FE80::1, up/up
PC-B on LAN 2: 2001:db8:26:1::20/64, gateway FE80::1
PC-B reaches FE80::1 locally; remote hosts have the intended two LAN prefixes.

prompt: Which two conclusions are supported, without claiming the router knows the cause of every failed test? Choose two.
options: A static route to either directly connected /64 is the missing prerequisite.
Successful local ping proves that R1 forwards between the LANs.
The LAN 1 host can resolve and reach its router as an endpoint.
The failure proves that the LAN 2 host has a duplicate IPv6 address.
IPv6 forwarding is missing even though both connected interfaces have addresses.
explanation: Local success and addressed interfaces establish less than transit success. The complete relevant configuration identifies the disabled forwarding prerequisite; no invented duplicate diagnosis is needed.

whyWrong.0: The prefixes are already connected; the explicit global forwarding setting is the missing prerequisite.
whyWrong.1: An endpoint reply is different from transit forwarding.
whyWrong.3: No DAD or duplicate evidence is supplied.

exhibit.title: Local replies without transit forwarding (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0: 2001:db8:28:1::1/64 up/up
R1 Gi0/1: 2001:db8:28:2::1/64 up/up
Global: no ipv6 unicast-routing; no filters
PCs have the matching /64 and their own on-link R1 gateway.
Each PC can ping its own R1 interface; PC-to-PC ping fails.
